paragraphs: Our syllabus asks us to sketch and interpret displacement time graphs. Read position and gradient, use a tangent on a curve, and separate distance from displacement.

scenes.text: Our syllabus asks us to sketch and interpret displacement time graphs. Read position and gradient, use a tangent on a curve, and separate distance from displacement.
A displacement time graph is a record of position. It shows where a particle is relative to a fixed origin as time passes.
Time runs across the graph. Displacement runs upward. Move the particle in the positive direction and the line rises. Every new point matches the particle's position at that instant.
The gradient tells us the velocity, a rising line gives positive velocity, a falling line gives negative velocity, and the steeper the line, the greater the speed.
A straight sloping line has constant gradient, so velocity is constant, a horizontal line has zero gradient, so the particle is at rest, a curve has a changing gradient, so velocity is changing.
On a curve, velocity changes from moment to moment. Draw a tangent at the instant you need. Its gradient is the instantaneous velocity. As the tangent pivots, the velocity readout changes with it.

Now move back toward the origin. The graph falls at zero displacement. The particle is at the origin. Continue past it. And displacement becomes negative. The arrow flips because the particle is now on the negative side. Distance itself has not become negative.

paragraphs: Consider a walker: from two metres, reach ten metres at four seconds; rest until six seconds; finish at minus six metres at ten seconds. [hold 2 s]
What is velocity? Gradient equals displacement change over time change. V equals delta s over delta t. [hold 2 s]

Let's draw. Start at two metres; reach ten metres after four seconds: two metres per second. [hold 2 s] Rest until six seconds. Reach minus six metres at ten seconds. Final velocity? Minus four metres per second. [hold 2 s]

paragraphs: Displacement? Finish minus start: delta s equals final s minus initial s. Here, minus eight metres. [hold 2 s] Distance? Add absolute changes on every leg. D equals their sum. Eight metres out, sixteen metres back: twenty four metres. [hold 2 s]

paragraphs: Average velocity? Displacement over time: v bar equals delta s over delta t. Ten seconds gives minus zero point eight metres per second. [hold 2 s] Average speed? Distance over time: D over delta t gives two point four metres per second. [hold 2 s] Velocity keeps direction; speed uses total distance.

paragraphs: Consider a cyclist: from rest, accelerate at one metre per second squared for two seconds. Cruise at two metres per second for three seconds; rest two seconds; return at minus two for four seconds. [hold 2 s]
Let's draw. Gradient equals displacement change over time change. Delta s over delta t equals velocity.
Accelerating: what changes? Two metres over two seconds: chord gradient, positive one. Tangent velocity rises from zero to two. Positive: away. [hold 2 s]
Cruising: what slope? Six metres over three seconds: positive two, constant. [hold 2 s]
Resting: what slope? Zero over two: zero, stationary. [hold 2 s]
Returning: predict the sign. [pause 3 s] Minus eight metres over four seconds: negative two, returning. [hold 2 s]
What if returning slower? Less steep, arriving later.

Rest 2 seconds, return at minus 2 for 4 seconds. Let's draw. Gradient equals displacement change over time change. Delta s over delta t equals velocity. Accelerating, what changes? Two metres over two seconds, chord gradient, positive one. Tangent velocity rises from zero to two. Positive, away. Cruising, what slope? Six metres over three seconds, positive two, constant. Resting, what slope? Zero over two, zero, stationary. Returning predict the sign. Minus eight metres over four seconds, negative two, returning. What if returning slower? Less steep, arriving later.

Recap. A displacement time graph shows signed position against time. Its gradient is velocity. Straight means constant velocity. Horizontal means rest. A curve needs a tangent for velocity at one instant. Add absolute position changes for distance. Use endpoint change for displacement. Then keep the averages separate.
